Experimental Male Contraceptive Pill Aims for On-Demand Use Within 30 Minutes

31 Oct 2026, 08:22 AM IST · GlobeWire Daily Science Desk · Source: news.abplive.com

Key takeawaysScientists at Weill Cornell Medicine in the United States are currently investigating an experimental non-hormonal birth control pill designed for men. The developmental drug targets sperm mobility rather than altering male hormone levels, offering a potential new appro

Scientists at Weill Cornell Medicine in the United States are currently investigating an experimental non-hormonal birth control pill designed for men. The developmental drug targets sperm mobility rather than altering male hormone levels, offering a potential new approach to family planning.

Unlike traditional hormonal contraceptives, this research focuses on temporarily inhibiting an enzyme known as soluble adenylyl cyclase (sAC). This specific enzyme plays a critical role in enabling sperm to swim effectively toward an egg for fertilization. By blocking sAC, the experimental medication aims to temporarily impair sperm movement for a duration lasting approximately six to eight hours.

Mechanism and Proposed Usage

According to early-stage studies, the proposed contraceptive is intended to be taken on-demand, roughly 30 minutes before sexual intercourse, rather than requiring daily administration. Researchers emphasize that the drug is not designed to halt overall sperm production. Instead, the body continues to produce sperm normally, while the medication temporarily restricts their ability to swim while active.

In October 2026, the research team secured additional funding designated for advanced toxicity and safety testing. This financial support marks a step toward preparing the candidate drug for potential human clinical trials.

Practical Implications and Reader Verification

Readers should note that this experimental treatment remains strictly in the pre-clinical research phase. Because testing has thus far been limited to animal models, such as mice, its safety, correct dosage, efficacy, and reversibility in humans are entirely unproven.

  • What is confirmed: Researchers are studying an sAC-inhibiting compound in laboratory settings to temporarily restrict sperm motility without affecting hormone levels or halting sperm production.
  • What remains unknown: Human efficacy rates, exact human dosage, long-term impact on male fertility, and whether normal sperm movement consistently returns after repeated use.
  • STI Protection: The experimental pill is strictly intended to prevent pregnancy and offers no protection against sexually transmitted infections (STIs).
